formation.title: The Mughal Throne
formation.text:
The Peacock Throne stands assembled, its gemstones catching the light of a subcontinent united under our banner. From the snowy passes of the Hindu Kush to the sweltering plains of the Ganges, our writ now runs. But what manner of empire shall this be? Babur conquered with thunder and horsemen: his legacy demands we press ever onward, subjugating all who resist the Mughal standard. Yet Akbar showed another path: a realm where Hindu and Muslim serve side by side, where the Ibadat Khana echoes with debate rather than dogma. The choice before us will define not just our reign, but the soul of the empire itself.

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: We shall conquer as Babur conquered!

modifiers.name: Sword of Babur
modifiers.text: The Mughal Empire was born from conquest. Babur rode down from the Afghan highlands with a hardened army and a will to carve a dynasty from Hindustan's plains. That spirit of relentless military expansion now infuses our armies, driving them to conquer what lesser empires could only covet.

options.text: We shall enlighten as Akbar enlightened.

modifiers.name: Light of Akbar
modifiers.text: Where others rule by the sword alone, Akbar understood that an empire spanning a hundred peoples must be built on something deeper than fear. His policy of sulh-i-kul, universal peace, wove Hindu, Muslim, Jain, and Zoroastrian into a single imperial tapestry. That tradition of synthesis now guides our realm toward wisdom and prosperity.

advances.name: Timurid Legacy
advances.text: The Mughals trace their lineage to Timur and Genghis Khan: a heritage of mounted conquest and imperial ambition that shaped their approach to ruling Hindustan.

advances.name: Chagatai Court Culture
advances.text: The Mughals brought the refined Persian literary tradition of the Chagatai courts to India, establishing a cosmopolitan culture of poetry, calligraphy, and courtly etiquette.

advances.name: Central Asian Horsemanship
advances.text: The steppe traditions of horse breeding and mounted warfare that the Mughals carried from Central Asia gave them an enduring advantage on the plains of Hindustan.

advances.name: Persian Administrative Heritage
advances.text: Mughal bureaucracy drew heavily on Persian models of governance: the diwan system, land revenue records, and a professional class of administrators writing in Persian script.

advances.name: Sufi Devotional Tradition
advances.text: Sufi saints and their khanqahs served as bridges between Islam and India's diverse spiritual landscape, winning converts through devotion and poetry rather than force.

advances.name: Babur's Gunpowder Revolution
advances.text: Babur's decisive deployment of Ottoman-style field artillery at Panipat in 1526 introduced a new era of gunpowder warfare to the Indian subcontinent.

event.title: The Thunder of Panipat
event.text: When Babur's small army faced the vast host of Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526, he deployed a weapon Hindustan had never seen used so decisively: massed field artillery behind a barricade of carts. The Lodi elephants and cavalry crashed against the wagons while Mughal cannons tore through their ranks. In a single morning, the Delhi Sultanate was shattered. Our military scholars now study Babur's tactics with renewed intensity. Shall we master the firepower that won us India, or perfect the cavalry charge that broke Lodi's flanks?

options.text: Let our cannons shake the earth.

modifiers.name: Legacy of Panipat: Firepower
modifiers.text: Our artillery corps carries forward the devastating innovation that won the Battle of Panipat.

options.text: Let our horsemen sweep the field.

modifiers.name: Legacy of Panipat: Horsemen
modifiers.text: Our cavalry embodies the swift, encircling tactics that shattered the Lodi host at Panipat.

advances.name: Karkhana Tradition
advances.text: The Mughal karkhanas were imperial workshops producing everything from brocade textiles and jewelry to weapons and saddles, all under the supervision of the Mir Saman.

advances.name: Mansabdari System
advances.text: Akbar's mansabdari system assigned numerical ranks (mansabs) to military and civil officials, determining their pay, troop obligations, and status within the imperial hierarchy.

advances.name: Patronage of Learning
advances.text: The Mughal court attracted scholars, historians, and scientists from across the Islamic world, funding translations of Sanskrit texts into Persian and advancing astronomy, mathematics, and medicine.

advances.name: Mughal Miniature Painting
advances.text:
The Mughal school of miniature painting blended Persian precision with Indian vivacity, producing masterworks under the patronage of emperors from Humayun to Shah Jahan.

Available in: Imperial Karkhana

advances.name: Mughal Urban Planning
advances.text: The Mughals built planned cities (Fatehpur Sikri, Shahjahanabad) with symmetrical gardens, public fountains, hammams, and sophisticated water management systems.

advances.name: Barqandaz Corps
advances.text: The barqandaz were professional matchlock musketeers, often recruited from specific clans and communities, who formed the backbone of Mughal infantry firepower.

advances.name: Topkhana Corps
advances.text: The topkhana was the centralized imperial artillery command, unique among Mughal military branches for being directly under the emperor's control rather than distributed among mansabdars.

advances.name: Revenue Reforms
advances.text: Akbar's finance minister Todar Mal introduced the zabt system: a standardized land revenue assessment based on measured acreage and average yields, replacing arbitrary tribute with predictable taxation.

advances.name: Sulh-i-Kul
advances.text: Akbar's principle of sulh-i-kul, peace with all, abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims, appointed Hindus to high office, and established the Ibadat Khana for interfaith dialogue.

event.title: Sulh-i-Kul: Universal Peace
event.text: In 1575, Emperor Akbar established the Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri: a House of Worship where Sunni ulama debated alongside Hindu Brahmins, Jain monks, Jesuit missionaries, and Zoroastrian priests. From these discussions emerged sulh-i-kul, Akbar's doctrine of universal peace. He abolished the jizya, appointed Hindus to the highest mansabs, and declared that no man should be molested on account of his faith. The empire's scholars now wrestle with the implications. Shall we embrace this radical tolerance as our governing philosophy, or channel the energy of reform into strengthening the sinews of the state?

options.text: All faiths shall find shelter under our canopy.

modifiers.name: Sulh-i-Kul: Peace with All
modifiers.text: Akbar's doctrine of universal tolerance attracts the loyalty of diverse peoples across the subcontinent.

options.text: Reform shall strengthen the hand of the Padshah.

modifiers.name: Sulh-i-Kul: Imperial Reform
modifiers.text: The energy of Akbar's reforms has been channeled into strengthening imperial administration and crown authority.

advances.name: Grand Trunk Road
advances.text: The Grand Trunk Road stretched over 2,500 kilometers from Chittagong to Kabul, connecting the empire's markets through a chain of sarais, toll stations, and caravanserais.

event.title: The Grand Trunk Road
event.text: Stretching over two thousand miles from Chittagong on the Bay of Bengal to Kabul in the Afghan highlands, the Grand Trunk Road is the spine of the Mughal Empire. Originally built by Sher Shah Suri and expanded under Mughal rule, it connects the empire's greatest cities (Delhi, Agra, Lahore, Peshawar) through a network of sarais, caravanserais, and toll stations. Merchants travel its length carrying muslin from Dhaka, spices from Gujarat, horses from Central Asia, and silver from Bengal. Our engineers have now completed major improvements to the road system, establishing imperial waystation networks that accelerate both trade and the movement of imperial decrees.

options.text: The road binds the empire together.

advances.name: Dhaka Muslin
advances.text:
The muslins of Dhaka were so fine they were called 'woven wind': a single bolt could be drawn through a finger ring. European traders paid fortunes for this fabric that no loom in the West could replicate.

Available in: Imperial Karkhana

advances.name: Ahadi Guard
advances.text: The Ahadi were elite gentleman troopers who served as the emperor's personal guard, handpicked for their skill at arms and personal loyalty, answering to no mansabdar but the Padshah himself.

advances.name: Mughal Engineering
advances.text: From the massive red sandstone walls of Agra Fort to the intricate water channels of Shalimar Gardens, Mughal engineers mastered both military fortification and hydraulic engineering.

advances.name: Jharokha-i-Darshan
advances.text: Each morning, the Mughal emperor appeared at the jharokha window to receive the assembled populace: a ritual that reinforced the sacred bond between ruler and subject across religious lines.

advances.name: Banduqchi Reforms
advances.text: As European military organization penetrated India, later Mughal commanders adopted more disciplined musketeer formations, the banduqchi, drilled in volley fire and coordinated maneuver.

advances.name: Mughal Textile Empire
advances.text:
By the 18th century, Indian textiles accounted for roughly a quarter of world manufacturing output. Mughal workshops produced silk brocades, fine muslin, chintz, and calico that clothed Europe, Africa, and Southeast Asia.

Available in: Imperial Karkhana

advances.name: Provincial Governance
advances.text: The nawabs, nizams, and subadars who governed Mughal provinces developed increasingly sophisticated local administrations: a double-edged sword that maintained order while enabling eventual autonomy.

advances.name: Renaissance of Letters
advances.text: Even as the empire's military power waned, its literary and scholarly traditions flourished: Urdu poetry, Persian histories, and Arabic theological works continued to emerge from Mughal courts and madrasas.

advances.name: Indigo and Opium Trade
advances.text: Mughal India's indigo plantations and opium production became major export industries, feeding European textile dyes and the expanding Asian opium market through the ports of Surat and Calcutta.

destiny.name: Destiny of the Mughals
destiny.text: The Mughal Empire has been proclaimed. Whether we pursue the path of conquest or enlightenment, the stability of the realm must first be secured before we can shape its destiny.

conditions.text: Stability at least 25

event.title: The Destiny of the Mughals
event.text: The Mughal throne is secure, the realm at peace. From Delhi to Lahore, from Agra to the mountain passes, our word is law. But a great empire does not stand still: it grows or it withers. The question now is not whether we shall act, but in what direction our ambition shall carry us.

destiny.name: Subjugate the Deccan
destiny.text: The Deccan sultanates of Golconda and Bijapur stand as independent powers on our southern frontier. To fulfill Babur's legacy of conquest, we must bring them under the Mughal standard and secure the wealth of the south.

conditions.text: Chose Sword of Babur
Own Golconda, or a subject owns it
Own Bijapur, or a subject owns it
Army size at least 30

event.title: The Deccan Brought to Heel
event.text: The Deccan sultanates, those proud remnants of the Bahmani kingdom, have at last been brought under Mughal authority. Golconda with its diamond mines and Bijapur with its fertile fields now pay tribute to the Peacock Throne. Our armies have proven that the mountain barriers of central India are no defense against Mughal resolve.

destiny.name: Conquer Bengal
destiny.text: The rich delta of Bengal (Sonargaon, Chittagong) controls access to the Bay of Bengal and produces the finest textiles in the world. A conquering empire must seize this wealth: the two ports and half of the province.

conditions.text: Own Sonargaon, or a subject owns it
Own Chittagong, or a subject owns it
Army size at least 50
We or our non-sovereign subjects hold at least 50% of the locations in Bengal

event.title: The Conquest of Bengal
event.text: Bengal has fallen to Mughal arms. The great river delta (source of the finest muslin, the richest rice harvests, and access to the eastern seas) is ours. Our generals now debate how best to consolidate these conquests. Some advocate an iron fist: aggressive expansion fueled by the spoils of war. Others counsel building the military roads and supply chains that will sustain further campaigns across the empire's vast distances.

options.text: Let the sword speak for the empire.

modifiers.name: The Iron Fist
modifiers.text: The momentum of conquest drives us forward. Wars are declared swiftly, and the exhaustion of campaigns weighs less heavily on a people accustomed to victory.

options.text: Build the roads that feed the armies.

modifiers.name: The Iron Road
modifiers.text: Military roads and supply depots sustain our armies across vast distances, though the focus on logistics leaves less room for diplomatic niceties.

destiny.name: Reclaim the Timurid Heartland
destiny.text: Babur wept for Samarkand, the jewel his family lost. The ultimate ambition of the Mughal dynasty is to reclaim the ancestral Timurid capitals (Samarkand, Herat, and Kandahar) and unite the empire of Timur with the empire of Hindustan.

conditions.text: Own Samarkand, or a subject owns it
Own Herāt, or a subject owns it
Own Kandahār, or a subject owns it
Army size at least 75
Prestige at least 75
Gold at least 3000

event.title: The Return to Samarkand
event.text: At last, a Mughal emperor stands in the Registan of Samarkand, fulfilling the dream that Babur carried to his grave. The ancestral lands of Timur, from Herat's minarets to Kandahar's fortress, fly the Mughal standard once more. This is the apex of empire, the union of two worlds: the refined civilization of Hindustan joined to the martial heritage of Central Asia. How shall we wield this unprecedented power?

options.text: We are the conquerors of the world.

modifiers.name: Conqueror of the World
modifiers.text: The Mughal military machine operates with devastating efficiency: storming fortresses, pressing advantages, and bringing battles to swift conclusion.

options.text: We are the emperors of an age.

modifiers.name: Emperor of an Age
modifiers.text: The empire's sheer scale and administrative reach allow it to field vast armies while minimizing the wastage of campaigning across diverse terrain.

destiny.name: The Jewel of Gujarat
destiny.text: Gujarat and its great port of Surat are the gateway to the Indian Ocean trade. Securing this region and establishing silk in our markets will lay the commercial foundation for a prosperous empire.

conditions.text: Chose Light of Akbar
Own Surat, or a subject owns it
A market the country is in

children.text: Silk is produced in the market
Silk is traded in the market

conditions.text: Gold at least 1000

event.title: Gujarat Secured
event.text: The port of Surat now flies the Mughal standard, and with it the commerce of the Arabian Sea flows into our treasury. Gujarat's merchant communities (Hindu banias, Muslim bohras, Parsi traders) bring the goods of the world to our doorstep. Silk, spices, and silver change hands in bustling markets that generate wealth beyond what conquest alone could ever yield.

options.text: The wealth of the world passes through our hands.

destiny.name: Workshop of the World
destiny.text: India produces a quarter of the world's manufactured goods. To realize this potential, the empire must strike its own silver in an imperial Zarb-khana and build up Agra, the seat of the imperial workshops, into a great city.

conditions.text: An Imperial Zarb-khana stands in one of our towns
We own Agra and its development is at least 54
Gold at least 2000

event.title: The Workshop Ascendant
event.text: India's artisans and merchants have made the Mughal Empire the manufacturing center of the known world. Our textiles clothe Europe and Africa, our indigo dyes color their fabrics, and our spices season their tables. The question is how best to nurture this economic miracle. Shall we pursue cultural synthesis: drawing the best minds of every tradition into our service? Or shall we empower our artisan guilds and open our markets to the world?

options.text: Synthesis of all traditions under our roof.

modifiers.name: Imperial Synthesis
modifiers.text: The Mughal court draws scholars, artists, and mystics from every tradition, radiating cultural influence across the region: though maintaining this cosmopolitan court does not come cheaply.

options.text: Let our artisans trade freely with the world.

modifiers.name: Artisan Freedom
modifiers.text: Freed from restrictive guild monopolies, Mughal artisans innovate and trade openly, driving recovery and growth across the empire's markets.

destiny.name: Padshah-i-Hind
destiny.text: The title Padshah-i-Hind, Emperor of All India, remains aspirational until the Mughal writ runs from the Malabar Coast to the tip of the subcontinent. Madurai and Kozhikode must acknowledge our supremacy, and Delhi must be rebuilt as a capital worthy of the title.

conditions.text: Own Madurai, or a subject owns it
Own Kozhikode, or a subject owns it
We own Delhi and its development is at least 82
Prestige at least 75
Gold at least 3000

event.title: Padshah-i-Hind
event.text: From the snow-capped passes of Kashmir to the palm-fringed coast of Malabar, from the bazaars of Surat to the temples of Madurai: the entire Indian subcontinent acknowledges the Mughal emperor as Padshah-i-Hind, Emperor of All India. No realm in the world commands such wealth, such diversity of peoples, or such depth of civilization. The Mughal court now debates how to consecrate this achievement. Shall we build an empire of spiritual harmony where all faiths flourish under our protection? Or shall we become the great marketplace of the world, where all nations come to trade?

options.text: An empire of harmony under heaven.

modifiers.name: Golden Age of Harmony
modifiers.text: The Mughal Empire stands as a beacon of interfaith harmony. Under the emperor's protection, mosques, temples, and churches flourish side by side. Subjects of other faiths are content, and converts are drawn through persuasion rather than coercion.

modifiers.name: World Market
modifiers.text: The Mughal Empire has become the hub of global commerce, managing vast trade networks that require sophisticated financial instruments. And the costs that come with them.

units.name: Barqandaz
units.text: Professional matchlock musketeers recruited from specialist communities, the barqandaz formed the firepower core of Mughal infantry. Their steady volleys covered the advance of imperial cavalry.

units.name: Barqandaz Levy
units.text: Levied matchlock infantry drawn from the empire's musketeer traditions.

units.name: Topkhana
units.text: The imperial Topkhana was the Mughal artillery corps: heavy bronze and iron cannons manned by specialized gunners under direct imperial command, devastating in siege and field alike.

units.name: Ahadi Guard
units.text: Elite household cavalry sworn to the emperor personally, the Ahadi were gentleman troopers selected for martial skill and loyalty, serving as shock cavalry in battle and as the emperor's mounted bodyguard.

units.name: Ahadi Levy
units.text: Levied imperial guard cavalry from the Ahadi tradition.

units.name: Banduqchi
units.text: Reformed musketeer infantry trained in European-style volley fire and linear tactics, the banduqchi represented the Mughal military's adaptation to the changing nature of warfare in the 18th century.

buildings.name: Imperial Karkhana
buildings.text: A state-run workshop producing luxury textiles, metalwork, and armaments under imperial supervision. The karkhana system centralized artisan production for the court and military.

buildings.name: Imperial Sarai
buildings.text: A fortified waystation along the imperial road network, providing shelter, fresh horses, and market access to merchants and official couriers traveling the Grand Trunk Road.

buildings.name: Maktab
buildings.text: An elementary Islamic school where children learn to read the Quran, study Persian grammar, and receive basic instruction in arithmetic and calligraphy: the foundation of Mughal literacy.

buildings.name: Imperial Hammam
buildings.text: A public bathhouse in the Persian tradition, serving as both a place of hygiene and a social institution where all classes mingled: a hallmark of Mughal urban civilization.

buildings.name: Topkhana Arsenal
buildings.text: A centralized facility for casting cannons, manufacturing firearms, and storing gunpowder: the logistical backbone of the Mughal empire's formidable artillery arm.

buildings.name: Imperial Zarb-khana
buildings.text: The imperial mint, where standardized Mughal coinage was struck in gold, silver, and copper: the backbone of a monetary system that facilitated trade across the subcontinent.

buildings.name: War Elephant Battery
buildings.text: A combined-arms facility where war elephants are trained alongside artillery crews, creating the devastating elephant-mounted cannon platforms that were a hallmark of Mughal military innovation.

buildings.name: Diwan-i-Am
buildings.text: The Hall of Public Audience: a grand pavilion where the emperor sits on an elevated throne to dispense justice, receive petitions, and display the magnificence of Mughal sovereignty to all who come before the Peacock Throne.

list.name: Mansabdari
list.text: Akbar's rank-grade military aristocracy, instituted in 1574 and refined under Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb. Every officer of the empire holds a dual rank, zat (his personal salary grade) and sawar (the cavalry contingent he is obliged to maintain), with ranks running from mansabdar of ten to the great commanders of seven thousand. The system marries Persian and Turkic warband traditions to a centrally-paid state, turning the entire nobility into rotatable, transferable, dismissable officers of the throne. Its decay in the late seventeenth century (bloated paper-rolls, jagir shortages, faction at court) is the textbook story of late-Mughal collapse.

list.name: Dahsala Settlement
list.text: Raja Todar Mal's ten-year revenue system, the Ain-i-Dahsala promulgated in 1582, which fixes the land-tax for a decade on the average crop-yield of the previous ten years, expressed in silver dams and converted to rupees. It is the first uniform, centrally-audited, cash-based revenue survey on the subcontinent, measured in the field by karoris (crown agents who survey holdings in bighas of the imperial standard). Predictable assessment breaks the bargaining power of the zamindars and feeds the imperial treasury without fail, but it leaves the peasant raiyat at the mercy of a rigid silver schedule when the harvest fails.

list.name: Diwan-i-Khalsa
list.text: The treasury of the imperial crown lands, distinct from the Diwan-i-Tan that pays mansabdar salaries. Khalsa territory is held in direct demesne (never assigned out as a jagir) with revenue flowing straight to the imperial hazana under the Diwan-i-Ala's audit. Akbar drastically expanded the khalsa share at the expense of assignment; Aurangzeb's Deccan wars reverse the trend, starving the khalsa to feed jagir obligations. The size of khalsa as a fraction of the realm is a direct dial of central versus aristocratic power, and the umara know it.

list.name: Jagirdari
list.text: The assignment of revenue-rights over a tract of land to a mansabdar in lieu of cash salary, transferable at the emperor's pleasure, typically every three to four years. By Akbari design jagirs are never hereditary; the rotation prevents the nobility from striking local roots and keeps the umara dependent on the throne's continuing favour. By the late Aurangzeb period the empire fields more mansabdars than there are jagirs to assign, the bejagiri crisis that produces the factionalism consuming the eighteenth century. The system rewards the noble class while transferring the cost of overextraction onto the peasant of a holding the assignee will soon leave.

list.name: Mir Bakshi's Office
list.text: The paymaster-general of the empire, head of the Diwan-i-Arz, who maintains the dagh (horse-branding) and chehra (descriptive roll of every soldier and his mount) the system relies on to keep mansabdars from presenting borrowed horses at muster. The Mir Bakshi audits every officer's contingent, runs the imperial intelligence service of waqia-navis (event-writers) reporting daily on each subah, and presents officers to the emperor for promotion. A functioning Mir Bakshi is the difference between the army the paper rolls promise and the army the throne can actually field at Panipat.

conditions.text: Has embraced Professional Armies

list.name: Imperial Karkhanas
list.text: The network of state-run manufactories (thirty-eight at Akbar's death, per Abu'l-Fazl's Ain-i-Akbari) that produces arms, armour, fine textiles, jewellery, illuminated manuscripts, and the splendid court goods that define Mughal majesty. The Buyutat-i-Khas administers them under the Khan-i-Saman, master of the imperial household; weavers from Gujarat, calligraphers from Iran, and gem-cutters from Golkonda are brought to Agra and Delhi to staff them. The karkhanas standardize quality across the empire and absorb the best hands from the bazaars, but their privileged supply contracts and conscripted masters squeeze the free urban guilds of Hindustan.

list.name: Sadr-us-Sudur
list.text: The empire's chief sadr, supreme judge in matters of Islamic law and overseer of madad-i-maash subsistence grants: rent-free land to scholars, sayyids, mosques, and madrasas, and after Akbar's reforms also to Hindu temples and Jain ascetics. Under Akbar and Jahangir the office is a vehicle of the sulh-i-kul (universal peace) policy, distributing patronage to non-Muslim clergy alongside the ulama. Under Aurangzeb it returns to a stricter Hanafi orientation, revoking many earlier grants. The sadr's tolerance dial directly sets the empire's relationship with its Hindu, Jain, Sikh, and Christian subjects.

list.name: Jharokha-i-Darshan
list.text: The daily public-audience ritual instituted by Akbar at the eastern jharokha, the latticed window of the imperial palace overlooking the Yamuna at Agra. Every dawn the Padshah presents himself to the assembled crowd, dispenses instant justice on petitions called up from the throng, and demonstrates by his sheer regular visibility that the throne is alive, watching, and approachable. Aurangzeb suspends the practice in his eleventh regnal year as un-Islamic quasi-divine display; contemporaries mark the suspension as the moment the throne loses its direct line to the people. The ritual bypasses the wakil and the umara hierarchy entirely.

conditions.text: Owns Agra
